# Associations between dermatologic immune-related adverse event morphologies and systemic immunomodulatory/immunosuppressive treatment: A large retrospective cohort study

**Authors:** Rachel M. Reardon; Katherine L. Perlman; Maria S. Asdourian; Nishi Shah; Ted V. Jacoby; Leah L. Thompson; Kerry L. Reynolds; Yevgeniy R. Semenov; Steven T. Chen

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Dermatology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | bHarvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | cUniversity of Illinois College of Medicine, Chicago, Illinois | dDivision of Hematology and Oncology, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center, Boston, Massachusetts

To the Editor: Among patients with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy, dermatologic immune-related adverse events (D-irAEs) are the earliest arising and most common irAEs. It remains challenging to optimize D-irAE management while pursuing overall oncology treatment goals.1,2 In this single-institution retrospective cohort study, we evaluate the relationships between distinct D-irAE morphologies and treatments utilized in their care.

Consistent with prior work,3 we used billing codes to identify patients who initiated ICI between January 1, 2016, and June 29, 2021 and developed D-irAEs treated at our institution. Manual chart review was used to abstract pertinent variables. The maximally potent treatment used in D-irAE-directed care for each D-irAE was categorized as systemically immunomodulating/immunosuppressive (n = 113), or not (n = 515). Associations between D-irAE morphologies and maximally potent treatments used/responses to those treatments were assessed using binomial logistic regression. All models were adjusted for age, sex, and baseline covariates significant to P < .05 (Table I). To address multiple hypothesis testing, we used the false discovery rate (FDR) control method with an FDR of 0.15.3

A total of 628 patients (median age 67 years, 40.9% female) were included. When adjusting for covariates, bullous (odds ratio [OR], 17.34; CI, 2.11-142.43; P = .008) and hypersensitivity (OR, 7.98; CI, 1.73-36.76; P = .008) morphologies displayed higher odds of receiving systemic immunosuppressive/immunomodulating treatment compared to nonspecific rashes (Table II). Psoriasiform D-irAEs had significantly higher odds of symptomatic improvement without a change in Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Event (CTCAE) grade (OR, 3.41; CI, 1.30-8.98; P = .01) and lower odds of improvement by a full CTCAE grade (OR, 0.31; CI, 0.12-0.84; P=.02) compared to nonspecific rashes, though the latter was not significant after FDR (Table II). Bullous and lichenoid D-irAEs displayed lower odds of improving by 2 or more CTCAE grades (OR, 0.02; CI, 0.001 – 0.75; P = .04 bullous; OR, 0.12; CI, 0.01-1.04; P = .05 lichenoid), though these differences were not significant after FDR (Table II).

In this retrospective cohort study, we evaluate relationships between specific D-irAE morphologies with use of systemic immunomodulation/immunosuppression and treatment responses. Lichenoid and psoriasiform D-irAEs are among the most common morphologies and are associated with survival benefits for cancer patients receiving ICI.1 Treatment guidelines center topical steroids for lower-grade eruptions and systemic steroids or biologics for more severe cases.1,2 After accounting for D-irAE severity, our results suggest that their improvement in response to maximally potent treatment may be limited. This provides important context for clinicians when discussing goals of dermatologic care in overall oncologic ICI treatment. Notably, bullous D-irAEs may have lower odds of improving by more than 1 CTCAE grade after maximally potent therapy including systemic corticosteroids (Supplementary Table III, available via Mendeley at https://doi.org/10.17632/36z655kjpt.1), contrasting prior work with a smaller cohort suggesting topical steroids are often sufficient for disease control.5

In spite of limitations including its retrospective single-institution design and use of electronic medical record data, this study presents important correlations between D-irAE morphologies with treatments utilized and D-irAE responses to those treatments. The survival benefits that may accompany bullous, psoriasiform, and lichenoid D-irAEs in the setting of ICI for cancer therapy1 should be balanced with their potential to persist despite potent therapy.
